never: Uses adverbs ending in -ly to modify dialogue tags (e.g., 'he said softly')
Uses the word 'very' as an intensifier
Uses chapter titles or numbered chapter headings in prose fiction (in Ulysses and Finnegans Wake)
Uses a omniscient narrator who editorializes morally about characters
Uses paragraph breaks to signal shifts in free indirect discourse
Uses standard question marks in interior monologue sequences (especially in Molly Bloom's soliloquy)
Uses apostrophes in contracted words in late style (e.g., 'cant' not "can't" in certain works)
Uses tidy plot resolution or closure
Uses said as a dialogue tag at all — dialogue attribution is typically omitted or replaced by dashes
Uses the em dash for interruption in the conventional way — instead uses a colon or run-on construction
Uses foreign words in italics — they appear in roman type
Uses exclamation points sparingly — they appear frequently and deliberately, not avoided but never used for authorial excitement, only character voice
Uses the passive voice as a default narrative register
Uses abstract Latinate diction when Anglo-Saxon or Irish vernacular will serve
Uses consistent tense — shifts between past and present within a single passage without signaling the shift
always: Opens dialogue with a long dash (—) rather than quotation marks
Embeds free indirect discourse without typographical signal, blending narrator and character voice mid-sentence
Uses the epiphany structure: accumulation of mundane detail resolving into a moment of sudden revelation
Catalogues proper nouns — street names, pub names, brand names, Dublin placenames — with documentary precision
Employs the interior monologue as a syntactically fragmented, associative, unpunctuated or minimally punctuated stream
Repeats a key word or phrase within a short passage as a rhythmic and thematic anchor
Uses the present participle heavily to create a sense of ongoing, unresolved action
Ends a climactic or emotionally weighted sentence with a monosyllable
Incorporates song lyrics, advertising slogans, and liturgical Latin into the narrative flow without quotation or attribution
Uses the colon to introduce lists, speech, or elaboration far more frequently than conventional prose
Builds sentences through accumulation of parallel noun phrases rather than subordinate clauses
Shifts register abruptly — from high literary diction to Dublin slang within a single paragraph
Uses onomatopoeia as a structural device, not merely decorative (e.g., 'Plop. Plop.' in Ulysses)
Employs the second person ('you') in interior monologue to represent a character's self-address
Uses short declarative sentences — sometimes single words — as paragraph-ending beats
Incorporates multilingual puns and portmanteau words, especially in Finnegans Wake
Structures longer works around mythological or literary parallels that are never explicitly named in the text
Uses the body and its functions as concrete, non-euphemistic narrative material
Repeats syntactic structures in threes for rhythmic emphasis
Grounds abstract emotion in a specific sensory detail — smell, texture, sound — rather than naming the emotion
